Chapter 3 introduces the Cox proportional hazards model, the central modelling tool
for relating survival experience to explanatory variables. These exercises cover the
formulation of the model, its fitting via partial likelihood, inference for hazard
ratios, model comparison and selection, and the interpretation and use of the fitted
model. Model checking (residuals and the proportional hazards assumption) is taken
up in Chapter 4.

## The Cox regression model  (Book §3.1–3.2)

### The hazard ratio

*Type: Concept & notation*

For two treatment groups, the proportional hazards model is $h_N(t) = \psi\, h_S(t)$,
where $h_N(t)$ and $h_S(t)$ are the hazards for the new and standard treatments.

(a) What does the quantity $\psi$ represent, and what does the value $\psi = 0.7$ mean
    in words?
(b) Why is $\psi$ re-expressed as $\exp(\beta)$? What is $\beta$ called, and what sign of
    $\beta$ corresponds to the new treatment being inferior?
(c) For $\beta = -0.3$, compute the hazard ratio and state which treatment is better.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) $\psi$ is the hazard ratio: the ratio of the hazard of death at time $t$ for an
    individual on the new treatment to that for an individual on the standard treatment,
    assumed constant over time. $\psi = 0.7$ means the hazard of death at any time is 30%
    lower on the new treatment, so the new treatment is better.
(b) The hazard ratio cannot be negative, so it is convenient to write $\psi = \exp(\beta)$;
    $\beta = \log\psi$ is the logarithm of the hazard ratio. $\beta$ can be any real value,
    and a positive $\beta$ gives $\psi > 1$, i.e. the new treatment is inferior.
(c) $\psi = \exp(-0.3) \approx 0.74$. Since the hazard ratio is below unity, the new
    treatment is better (lower hazard).
:::

### The baseline hazard and the linear component

*Type: Concept & notation*

The general Cox model for the hazard of the $i$th individual is

$$h_i(t) = \exp(\beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi})\, h_0(t).$$

(a) What is $h_0(t)$, and for whom is it the hazard?
(b) Why does the linear component contain no intercept (constant) term $\beta_0$?
(c) The quantity $\eta_i = \beta_1 x_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{pi}$ has two other names.
    What are they, and how is $\eta_i$ used to compare two individuals?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) $h_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard — the hazard for an individual for whom all the
    explanatory variables equal zero. In a model containing only a treatment indicator,
    it is the hazard in the reference group.
(b) If a constant $\beta_0$ were included, the baseline hazard could simply be rescaled
    (divided by $\exp(\beta_0)$) and the constant would cancel out, so $\beta_0$ is not
    identifiable and is absorbed into $h_0(t)$.
(c) The linear component is also called the *risk score* or *prognostic index*. The ratio
    of hazards for two individuals $i$ and $k$ is $\exp(\eta_i - \eta_k)$, so the risk
    score orders individuals by their hazard — a higher score means a higher hazard.
:::

### Fitting a factor

*Type: From research question to model*

A study of survival after kidney cancer (hypernephroma) records two factors: age group
($< 60$, $60$–$70$, $> 70$) and whether a nephrectomy was performed (no / yes).

(a) How many indicator (dummy) variables are needed to fit age group as a factor, and
    why? How many degrees of freedom does the factor have?
(b) Taking age group $< 60$ and "no nephrectomy" as the baseline levels, describe in
    words the patient to whom the baseline hazard $h_0(t)$ corresponds.
(c) Write the model for the hazard of a patient aged $> 70$ who had a nephrectomy, in
    terms of the relevant coefficients.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) A factor with three levels needs two indicator variables (e.g. $A_2 = 1$ if $60$–$70$,
    $A_3 = 1$ if $> 70$); the third level is the baseline. The factor has $3 - 1 = 2$
    degrees of freedom. In general an $m$-level factor needs $m-1$ parameters.
(b) The baseline hazard corresponds to a patient in the youngest age group ($< 60$) who
    did not have a nephrectomy, since all indicator variables are then zero.
(c) With coefficients $\alpha_2$ ($60$–$70$), $\alpha_3$ ($> 70$) and $\nu$
    (nephrectomy), the hazard is $\exp(\alpha_3 + \nu)\, h_0(t)$.
:::

### Proportional hazards and the semi-parametric model

*Type: Assumptions*

*Builds on: Chapters 1–2*

(a) In your own words, state the proportional hazards assumption underlying the Cox
    model, and say what kind of behaviour it rules out.
(b) The baseline hazard $h_0(t)$ is left completely unspecified — no distributional
    assumption is made about it. Why is the Cox model therefore called semi-parametric?
(c) Why does leaving $h_0(t)$ unspecified still allow the $\beta$-coefficients (and hence
    the hazard ratios) to be estimated?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) Proportional hazards means the effect of each covariate is a constant multiplicative
    factor on the hazard at every time $t$: the hazard for an individual is
    $\exp(\beta'x)$ times the baseline at all $t$. It rules out covariate effects that
    change (or reverse) over time — e.g. a treatment that helps early but harms later.
(b) The "parametric" part is the assumed exponential form of the covariate effects
    (the $\beta$s), while the "non-parametric" part is the unspecified baseline hazard
    $h_0(t)$. Hence semi-parametric.
(c) In the partial likelihood, $h_0(t)$ cancels from numerator and denominator at each
    event time, so the $\beta$s can be estimated using only the rank order of the
    survival times, without estimating $h_0(t)$.
:::

## Fitting the model and making inferences  (Book §3.3–3.5)

### The partial likelihood and the risk set

*Type: Risk set reasoning*

*Builds on: Chapter 2*

Five patients are followed. Patients 2 and 5 are right-censored, and the three deaths,
in order, are patients 3, 1 and 4 at times $t_{(1)} < t_{(2)} < t_{(3)}$. Patient 5 is
censored before $t_{(2)}$, and patient 2 between $t_{(2)}$ and $t_{(3)}$. Write
$\psi(i) = \exp(\beta'x_i)$.

(a) List the risk set at each of the three death times.
(b) Write the partial likelihood as a product over the three death times.
(c) Censored patients contribute no term to the numerator of the partial likelihood.
    Where does their information enter, and what does this imply about which feature of
    the data drives the estimate of $\beta$?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) $R(t_{(1)}) = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ (all five); $R(t_{(2)}) = \{1, 2, 4\}$ (patient 3
    has died, patient 5 censored); $R(t_{(3)}) = \{4\}$ (patient 1 has died, patient 2
    censored).
(b) $L(\beta) = \dfrac{\psi(3)}{\psi(1)+\psi(2)+\psi(3)+\psi(4)+\psi(5)}
    \times \dfrac{\psi(1)}{\psi(1)+\psi(2)+\psi(4)} \times \dfrac{\psi(4)}{\psi(4)}$.
(c) Censored individuals enter through the denominators (the risk sets) at death times
    that occur before their censoring time. Because $L(\beta)$ depends only on the
    ordering of the death times — which determines the risk sets — inference about
    $\beta$ depends only on the rank order of the survival times, not their actual values.
:::

### Interpreting Cox regression output

*Type: Interpret R output*

For the breast cancer data (Example 1.2 in the book), a Cox model with staining indicator $X$
($1$ = positive, $0$ = negative) gives $\hat\beta = 0.908$ with
$\mathrm{se}(\hat\beta) = 0.501$.

(a) Compute the estimated hazard ratio and interpret it in words.
(b) Compute a 95% confidence interval for the log hazard ratio $\beta$, and hence for
    the hazard ratio. Why is the interval obtained by exponentiating the $\beta$-limits
    preferable to $\hat\psi \pm 1.96\, \mathrm{se}(\hat\psi)$?
(c) The null model has $-2\log\hat L = 173.968$ and the model with $X$ has $170.096$.
    Carry out the likelihood-ratio test and interpret. (The corresponding log-rank test
    gave $\chi^2 = 3.515$, $P = 0.061$.)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) $\hat\psi = \exp(0.908) = 2.48$. The hazard of death at any time for a woman with a
    positively stained tumour is about 2.5 times that for a negatively stained woman;
    positive staining indicates a poorer prognosis.
(b) A 95% CI for $\beta$ is $0.908 \pm 1.96 \times 0.501 = (-0.074,\, 1.890)$.
    Exponentiating gives $(0.93,\, 6.62)$ for the hazard ratio. The log hazard ratio is
    closer to normally distributed than the hazard ratio itself, so exponentiating the
    $\beta$-limits gives a better-behaved interval.
(c) The difference is $173.968 - 170.096 = 3.872$ on 1 degree of freedom, giving
    $P = 0.049$. There is evidence, just significant at the 5% level, of a difference in
    hazard between the staining groups — essentially the same conclusion as the log-rank
    test ($P = 0.061$); the small difference in p-values is immaterial.
:::

### Interpreting a multi-variable model

*Type: Interpret R output*

For the multiple myeloma data (Example 1.3 in the book), a Cox model is fitted with all seven
explanatory variables. Of the individual 95% confidence intervals, only those for Bun
($\hat\beta = 0.021$, $\mathrm{se} = 0.006$) and Hb ($\hat\beta = -0.135$,
$\mathrm{se} = 0.069$) exclude zero. When Bun is omitted, the estimated coefficient of
Hb changes from $-0.135$ to $-0.140$, and the other coefficients change too.

(a) Why can we *not* conclude from these individual results alone that only Bun and Hb
    are needed in the model?
(b) What does the change in the estimated coefficients when Bun is omitted tell us about
    the estimates?
(c) In a model with several variables, what does it mean to say that a coefficient is
    "adjusted for" the others?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) Each individual Wald test tests $\beta_j = 0$ *in the presence of all the other
    variables*, and the estimates are correlated with one another. A variable's
    coefficient can change when another is removed, so the relevant subset cannot be
    identified from a single full model.
(b) It shows the estimates depend on which other variables are in the model (the
    variables are correlated), so each term's effect must be studied by comparing
    models, not by inspecting one full fit in isolation.
(c) "Adjusted for" the other variables means the estimated effect of a variable holds
    the other variables in the model fixed — it is the effect on the hazard controlling
    for the others.
:::

### Comparing nested models

*Type: Model comparison*

For the hypernephroma data (Example 3.4), the values of $-2\log\hat L$ for five nested
models are summarised below. Age group is fitted via $A_2, A_3$ and nephrectomy via $N$;
the interaction uses the products $A_2 N, A_3 N$.

| Terms in model | Variables | $-2\log\hat L$ |
|---|---|---|
| none | — | 177.667 |
| age group | $A_2, A_3$ | 172.172 |
| nephrectomy | $N$ | 170.247 |
| age group + nephrectomy | $A_2, A_3, N$ | 165.508 |
| + interaction | $A_2, A_3, N, A_2 N, A_3 N$ | 162.479 |

(a) Test for an interaction between age group and nephrectomy. What do you conclude?
(b) Does age group add to a model that already contains nephrectomy? Does nephrectomy
    add to a model that already contains age group?
(c) Which model would you select, and why? What role do the degrees of freedom play in
    these comparisons?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) The interaction reduces $-2\log\hat L$ by $165.508 - 162.479 = 3.029$ on 2 d.f.,
    $P = 0.220$, which is not significant. There is no evidence of an interaction: the
    effect of nephrectomy does not depend on age group.
(b) Age group added to nephrectomy: $170.247 - 165.508 = 4.739$ on 2 d.f.
    ($P = 0.094$), some evidence. Nephrectomy added to age group:
    $172.172 - 165.508 = 6.664$ on 1 d.f. ($P = 0.010$), significant. So nephrectomy is
    clearly needed, and age group adds something in the presence of nephrectomy.
(c) Select the model with both main effects and no interaction: the hazard depends on
    both age group and nephrectomy. The degrees of freedom are the difference in the
    number of parameters between the two nested models, which is the degrees of freedom
    of the chi-squared distribution of the difference in $-2\log\hat L$.
:::

## Model selection  (Book §3.6–3.8)

### A strategy for model selection

*Type: Method selection*

(a) State the hierarchic principle, and give an example of a situation where it applies.
(b) Why does the book recommend against relying uncritically on automatic forward
    selection, backward elimination or stepwise procedures?
(c) Describe the first step of the recommended model-selection strategy, and explain why
    a relatively large significance level (about 15%) is suggested for guiding inclusion.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) The hierarchic principle: a higher-order term (e.g. an interaction) should be
    included only when the corresponding lower-order (main effect) terms are present;
    otherwise the model is difficult to interpret. For example, an interaction between
    age group and nephrectomy is only interpretable when both main effects are fitted.
(b) Automatic routines typically return a single "best" subset rather than a set of
    equally good models; the result depends on the direction (forward, backward,
    stepwise) and on the stopping rule; and they generally ignore the hierarchic
    principle.
(c) Step 1 fits each variable alone and compares its $-2\log\hat L$ with that of the
    null model, to find which variables on their own significantly reduce the statistic.
    A generous level (about 15%) avoids excluding potentially relevant variables too
    early, since a variable unimportant on its own may become important in the presence
    of others.
:::

### Variable selection with the lasso

*Type: Method selection*

(a) What does the lasso do to the estimated coefficients, and how does it carry out
    variable selection?
(b) Why must the explanatory variables be standardised before the lasso is applied?
(c) How is the optimal value of the tuning parameter $\lambda$ chosen, and why are
    standard errors and hazard ratios usually not reported after using the lasso?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) The lasso shrinks the coefficients towards zero by penalising the sum of their
    absolute values (the $L_1$-norm); some are set exactly to zero, so the corresponding
    variables are excluded. The variables selected are those with non-zero coefficients.
(b) The penalty $\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|$ treats all coefficients on the same footing, so
    the variables must be on comparable scales; otherwise the penalty falls unequally on
    variables with large versus small measurement scales.
(c) $\lambda$ is chosen by, for example, cross-validation — maximising the
    cross-validated partial log-likelihood. Standard errors are usually not reported
    because the lasso estimates are biased towards zero, so their standard errors are
    not meaningful and would understate the precision of the estimates.
:::

## Interpreting and using the fitted model  (Book §3.9–3.11)

### Adjusted and unadjusted hazard ratios

*Type: What's wrong here?*

For the prostatic cancer data (Example 1.4), a model containing only the treatment
indicator gives a coefficient of $-1.978$ (hazard ratio $0.14$). After adjusting for
tumour size and Gleason index, the coefficient is $-1.113$ (hazard ratio $0.329$).

(a) Explain in words what the two hazard ratios estimate, and why they differ.
(b) A researcher reports "treatment reduces the hazard of death by 86%", based on the
    unadjusted model. What is wrong with this statement?
(c) Which hazard ratio is the better summary of the treatment effect, and why?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) The unadjusted hazard ratio ($0.14$) compares the treatment groups ignoring tumour
    size and Gleason index; the adjusted hazard ratio ($0.329$) compares two individuals
    on different treatments who have the same size and index. They differ because the
    prognostic variables are not equally distributed across the treatment groups, so the
    unadjusted comparison conflates the treatment effect with those differences.
(b) "86% reduction" overstates the effect: it is based on the unadjusted value, which is
    confounded by tumour size and grade. Properly adjusted, the reduction is about 67%
    (hazard ratio $0.33$) — still substantial, but less extreme.
(c) The adjusted hazard ratio, because it isolates the treatment effect from the effects
    of size and index. The aim is to estimate the effect of treatment, not the combined
    effect of treatment plus any imbalance in prognostic factors.
:::

### Estimating the survivor function

*Type: Concept & notation*

*Builds on: Chapter 2*

After fitting a Cox model, the estimated survivor function for an individual is

$$\hat S_i(t) = \big\{\hat S_0(t)\big\}^{\exp(\hat\beta'x_i)}.$$

(a) What is $\hat S_0(t)$, and how is $\hat S_i(t)$ obtained from it?
(b) With no covariates in the model, show that this formula reduces to the Kaplan–Meier
    estimate.
(c) In the hypernephroma example, nephrectomy has coefficient $-1.412$. If the baseline
    survivor function at 12 months is $\hat S_0(12) = 0.486$, estimate the 12-month
    survival probability for a patient aged $< 60$ who had a nephrectomy, and explain
    why the two estimated curves cannot cross.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) $\hat S_0(t)$ is the estimated baseline survivor function (for an individual with
    all covariates equal to zero). $\hat S_i(t)$ raises it to the power
    $\exp(\hat\beta'x_i)$, the individual's estimated hazard ratio relative to baseline.
(b) With no covariates, $\exp(\hat\beta'x_i) = 1$ and $\hat S_i(t) = \hat S_0(t)$, which
    equals the Kaplan–Meier estimate $\prod (n_j - d_j)/n_j$. So the Cox-based estimate
    generalises the Kaplan–Meier estimate to the case with covariates.
(c) $\hat S(12) = 0.486^{\exp(-1.412)} = 0.486^{0.244} \approx 0.84$. Because of
    proportional hazards the two survivor functions are powers of one another, so one is
    always above the other and they never cross; the nephrectomy curve lies above
    (nephrectomy improves prognosis).
:::

## Mini-lab: fitting a Cox model in R

### Fitting a Cox model in R

*Type: Mini-lab*

Run the code below. It simulates 200 patients with a treatment indicator (`treat`) and
age, generates survival times with a proportional-hazards structure, censors them, and
fits a Cox model.

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(2718)
n <- 200
treat <- rep(c(0, 1), each = n / 2)
age <- round(runif(n, 45, 80))
eta <- 0.55 * treat + 0.04 * (age - 60)
t <- rexp(n, rate = 0.08 * exp(eta))
cens <- runif(n, 0, 60)
obs <- pmin(t, cens)
status <- as.numeric(t <= cens)
d <- data.frame(time = obs, status = status, treat = treat, age = age)

library(survival)
fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treat + age, data = d)
summary(fit)
```

(a) From the summary, report the estimated hazard ratio and its 95% confidence interval
    for treatment, and interpret.
(b) Report the hazard ratio per additional year of age, and interpret.
(c) How many events are there? What does the "Concordance" line measure, and is the
    model useful for discrimination?
(d) What are the three tests at the bottom of the output, and do they agree?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="solutions"}
**Solution.**

(a) The hazard ratio for `treat` is $1.90$ (95% CI $1.38$ to $2.61$). The hazard of the
    event at any time is about 1.9 times as high for treated versus untreated patients,
    adjusted for age ($P < 0.001$).
(b) The hazard ratio per additional year of age is $1.038$ (95% CI $1.022$ to $1.054$);
    each extra year increases the hazard by about 3.8%.
(c) There are 172 events. Concordance (the $c$-statistic) is $0.60$, which is modest:
    the model separates higher- from lower-risk individuals only weakly (0.5 means no
    discrimination; values above about 0.7 are generally considered reasonable).
(d) The likelihood ratio, Wald and score (log-rank) tests all test the joint hypothesis
    that both coefficients are zero. They all give $P < 0.0001$, strongly rejecting the
    null — the three tests agree.
:::
